summary.text: A wave function is a mathematical description of the quantum state of an isolated quantum system, usually written with the Greek letters ψ and Ψ.
It assigns a complex number to each point, and the Born rule turns its squared size into the probability of finding a particle at a given place.
The Schrödinger equation sets how wave functions change over time, and its wave-like math explains the name and gives rise to wave-particle duality.

facts.label: Usual symbol
facts.value: The Greek letters ψ and Ψ, lower-case or capital

facts.label: Normalization
facts.value: The total squared size over all possibilities must equal 1

facts.label: Complex-valued
facts.value: Each point gets a complex number, not a plain one

facts.label: Position or momentum
facts.value: A Fourier transform converts between the two versions

facts.label: Spin included
facts.value: For electrons and photons it carries spin as a discrete variable

items.prompt: A wave function assigns a complex number to each point in space. How do you get the chance of finding the particle near a point?

options.label: Square the size of the complex number at that point
Take the number's real part and add one
Add up the numbers at every nearby point
Read off the number directly as a percentage

items.explain: The Born rule says the squared modulus of a position wave function is the probability density of finding the particle there.

items.prompt: A friend normalizes a wave function and checks that all the squared values over every possibility add up to 2. What went wrong?

options.label: Nothing, since totals can be any size
Nothing, because probabilities may exceed one
The total should be exactly 1, so it is not normalized
The total should be 0, so the function vanishes

items.explain: The integral of the squared modulus over all degrees of freedom must equal 1, a condition called normalization.

items.prompt: Why is a wave function called a 'wave' function?

options.label: It always describes a literal water wave
Its evolution follows an equation mathematically like other wave equations
It measures the height of the sea around particles
It was named after its inventor, a man called Wave

items.explain: The Schrödinger equation is mathematically akin to those for water waves or waves on a string, which explains the name.

items.prompt: Does the wave function description settle that it is a physical thing, like a water wave?

options.label: Yes, it is just a real physical wave in space
Yes, but only for photons, not electrons
No, it is only a stand-in for temperature
It is still open to different interpretations

items.explain: Whether the wave function describes a kind of physical phenomenon is still open to different interpretations, unlike classical mechanical waves.

items.prompt: You have a wave function in terms of position and want one in terms of momentum. What do you use?

options.label: A Fourier transform
A simple unit conversion
A new experiment each time
Nothing, only position is possible

items.explain: Information in a position wave function can be converted to a momentum one, and vice versa, by a Fourier transform.

items.prompt: Schrödinger first thought a wave function showed a particle smeared out in space. Why did this fail?

options.label: Particles cannot be found anywhere in space
A wave packet off a target spreads in all directions, unlike a particle
The wave function was too small to measure
It contradicted the speed of light in a vacuum

items.explain: This view was incompatible with elastic scattering of a wave packet, which spreads out in all directions.
